metaDescription: Six cordless pole hedge trimmers at or under $150, compared on blade length, reach, head angles and battery packs for tall hedges without a ladder.
expertTake: The BLACK+DECKER 20V pole trimmer is the best overall buy, because an 18-inch dual-action blade, a pivoting head and a battery in the box add up to a proven design. The TaskStar is the value pick for long reach and a shoulder strap. Anyone trimming thick overgrown privet should skip pole trimmers and use loppers or a gas machine.
introParagraphs: A pole hedge trimmer puts a blade on a long shaft so you can reach the top of a tall hedge from the ground. The tradeoff is weight at the tip, which tires your arms faster than a handheld trimmer.
Blade gap, head angles, pole length and battery strategy matter more than headline reach. Prices move, and the $150 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 20V MAX Pole Hedge Trimmer 18-Inch
products.description:
The BLACK+DECKER is a conventional, well-understood pole trimmer. An 18-inch dual-action blade cuts on both strokes, which means less vibration and smoother cuts than a single-action blade. The head pivots through 180 degrees, so you can cut a flat top from the side and a vertical face from below.

It ships with a battery and charger, which matters because the pack is the most expensive part of a cordless tool. The 20V MAX label refers to peak voltage, and the nominal system is 18V, which is typical for light hedges. Compared with the 16-inch trimmers, the longer blade makes fewer passes but puts more weight at the tip.

A single battery limits large jobs, so plan breaks. Keep the blade clean and oiled after each use, because resin buildup is the main cause of stalling. It is the choice for a standard suburban hedge. Take regular breaks, because the shoulders tire first.
pros: Pivoting head reaches flat tops and sides
cons: Long blade adds tip weight on a pole

products.name: TaskStar 20V Pole Hedge Trimmer 16-Inch 8.5 ft Reach
products.description:
The TaskStar offers a 16-inch blade on a pole with a claimed 8.5 feet of reach and a shoulder strap. A strap is a real ergonomic feature on a pole tool, because it moves part of the weight to your shoulder and steadies the tip.

The 8.5 ft reach figure probably includes some of the user's arm height, so the real working range is smaller. Compared with the BLACK+DECKER, the blade is shorter, which makes it easier to control at full extension.

Check the battery contents on the listing and keep the blade lubricated. It suits taller hedges where a strap helps. Before you buy extra batteries, check that the charger is a fast one, because waiting three hours between sessions ruins a weekend afternoon. Keep the blade oiled and the vent slots clear. A practical tip is to trim the sides first, then the top, so clippings fall onto cut areas you can sweep up in one go.
products.bestFor: Taller hedges where a strap reduces fatigue.
pros: Shorter blade is easier to control
cons: Reach claim likely includes arm height

products.name: MITLEX 40V Pole Hedge Trimmer 16-Inch 2 x 2.0Ah
products.description:
The MITLEX is the only 40V pole trimmer in the group. Higher voltage lets the blade hold its speed under load, which helps when a branch is at the upper end of the cutting capacity. It includes two 2.0Ah packs and a charger.

The packs are small in capacity, but at 40V they store more energy than 2.0Ah at 20V. Check the compatibility of the platform with other tools, since the brand is less common.

Keep the blade clear of resin. Because the platform is less common, confirm that replacement packs and blades are available before you commit, and keep the packaging so you can return it if the fit is wrong. Higher voltage also means higher blade speed, so wear gloves and eyewear. Think of it as the stronger choice for old, woody hedges that have been trimmed only occasionally.
products.bestFor: Thicker branches that stall a 20V trimmer.
pros: Two packs and a charger included

products.name: SOARFLY 2-in-1 Pole Hedge Trimmer 2 x 4.0Ah
products.description:
The SOARFLY detaches from its pole to become a handheld trimmer, a useful trick if you need to shape a low hedge or sculpt a shrub. The head rotates 150 degrees through eleven positions, giving the most angle choices in the group.

Two 4.0Ah batteries and a charger ship with it, which makes it a complete kit. Detachable designs tend to have a bit more flex in the joint, so full extension feels less rigid.

Keep the connection clean and the blade oiled. When you use it as a handheld, lock the pole joint firmly and keep fingers clear of the blade. The spare battery lets you swap rather than wait, and the many angle positions let you keep wrists straight. The ability to detach the head from the pole is useful in winter when you want to shape a small shrub near the door.
products.bestFor: Gardeners who want pole and handheld modes.
cons: Some flex at the pole joint

products.name: MZK 20V 2-in-1 Pole Hedge Trimmer and Grass Shear 13 ft
products.description:
The MZK claims the longest reach in the group at 13 feet and converts into a grass shear. Reach figures usually include the user's height, so treat it as a ceiling.

Its 1/2-inch cutting capacity is below the 5/8 to 3/4 inch of other trimmers, which limits it to softer growth. Two 4Ah packs and a multi-angle head make it versatile.

Store the batteries indoors. At full extension a very long pole flexes, so cut slowly and use short strokes, and do not try to reach beyond what you can see. Never use it from a ladder; a pole is the reason you do not need one. Because grass shears are a different blade, keep the right one fitted for the job and do not force the hedge blade through turf.
products.bestFor: Very tall hedges with soft growth.

products.name: CRAFTSMAN V20 Cordless Pole Hedge Trimmer 18-Inch Tool Only
products.description:
The CRAFTSMAN is a bare tool, so a V20 battery and charger must be supplied. It offers an 18-inch dual-action blade rated for up to 3/4 inch branches and a head that pivots 180 degrees through five positions.

For anyone with V20 batteries it is an economical add-on. Without them, price the full setup.

Keep the blade clean. Be careful to confirm which battery pack fits before ordering, because V20 packs are not interchangeable with older 20V designs. Add the cost of a pack to your plan, and a spare is worth considering. Add a spare blade guard to your list, since the sharp teeth need covering in storage.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The blade gap sets the thickest branch it can take. The CRAFTSMAN lists 3/4 inch and the MZK 1/2 inch. Branches thicker than the gap stall the blade, so use loppers for those. Check how the pole locks: a twist lock that slips is a common annoyance, while a clamp lock holds better. Use a drop cloth under the hedge to catch clippings, which cuts cleanup time. Check the bag of extras too, since a blade cover and wrench make the first season easier.

Claims like 13 feet on the MZK and 8.5 feet on the TaskStar usually add your arm height. The pole itself is shorter. Estimate your hedge height first. Add a face shield or glasses, because clippings fly upward when you cut overhead. Test the lock on the pole before every session, since a slip at full reach is dangerous. Prefer a model with a rubber grip, which reduces blisters on a long session.

A pole tool is tip-heavy, and an 18-inch blade adds more than a 16-inch one. Shoulder straps like the TaskStar's help reduce fatigue. If you share a battery family with other tools, a bare tool can be the cheapest route. Look at warranty length, since a pole tool takes more knocks than a handheld.

The SOARFLY offers eleven positions, the CRAFTSMAN five. More detents let you cut flat tops from the side and keep your neck neutral. Choose a blade length by how much of the hedge you can reach comfortably, not by the longest listed number. If you are short, pick a lighter blade and a shorter pole so you can keep control.

The CRAFTSMAN is tool only, while others ship packs. A pack can cost as much as the tool, so compare complete setups. Try to cut in dry conditions, since wet foliage clogs the blade and stalls small motors. Make sure the charger is rated for your wall outlet and sits flat on a shelf.

The MITLEX is 40V, others 20V. Higher voltage holds blade speed in thicker growth but needs a compatible platform. Look for a hand guard and a two-step trigger to reduce accidental starts. Trim in dry weather, because wet leaves clog the blade and stall the motor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutting capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared blade gap and length. The CRAFTSMAN at 3/4 inch led. Smaller gaps lost points. Blade capacity set the baseline for the ranking because it decides which hedges a tool can actually handle. The final order reflects how each trimmer behaves after twenty minutes of use, not in the first minute.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ergonomics
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at straps, blade length and head angles. The TaskStar strap and SOARFLY positions scored high. Ergonomic features like straps and head positions were weighted heavily since pole tools tire the user quickly. Reach, capacity and weight were all balanced against one another, since improving one often hurts another.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit contents
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked batteries and chargers. Tool-only listings were flagged. We compared what each kit includes, because a missing battery changes the true cost.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach realism
howWeEvaluated.description: We discounted reach claims that likely include arm height. Where reach claims looked inflated, we ranked the tool on pole length and blade control instead.

howWeEvaluated.title: Support
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed brand and parts. Owner feedback patterns informed the durability view. Warranty, parts and brand history counted toward the support score.

faq.q: How thick a branch can a pole hedge trimmer cut?
faq.a: Typically 1/2 to 3/4 inch. Anything thicker needs loppers or a pole saw. A thick branch is better cut with a pole saw than forced through a hedge blade.
